\begin{proof}
Let

R=\mathbb Z[x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots],\qquad K=(x_{2k+1}x_{2k+2}\mid k\ge 0).
\]
For every choice function \(\lambda:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\bigcup_{k\ge0}\{x_{2k+1},x_{2k+2}\}\), with \(\lambda(k)\in\{x_{2k+1},x_{2k+2}\}\), define
\[
I_\lambda=(\lambda(k)\mid k\ge0).
\]
There are infinitely many such choices, and distinct choices give distinct ideals. Since every generator of \(K\) has one factor in \(I_\lambda\), we have \(K\subseteq I_\lambda\).

The quotient \(R/I_\lambda\) is a polynomial ring over \(\mathbb Z\), hence an integral domain. Therefore \(I_\lambda/K\) is a prime ideal of \(R/K\).

Suppose \(J/K\subseteq I_\lambda/K\) is a prime ideal of \(R/K\). For each \(k\), the product \(x_{2k+1}x_{2k+2}\) lies in \(J\), so primality implies that one of its factors lies in \(J\). Because \(J\subseteq I_\lambda\), the factor must be \(\lambda(k)\). Thus every generator \(\lambda(k)\) of \(I_\lambda\) lies in \(J\), so \(I_\lambda\subseteq J\). Hence \(J=I_\lambda\), and consequently \(J/K=I_\lambda/K\).

Thus \(I_\lambda/K\) is a minimal prime ideal of \(R/K\) for every \(\lambda\). Since there are infinitely many distinct \(\lambda\), the ring contains infinitely many minimal prime ideals.
\end{proof}

\]
Each \(I_\lambda\) contains \(K\), since every generator \(x_{2k+1}x_{2k+2}\) is divisible by \(\lambda_k\). The quotient \(R/I_\lambda\) is a polynomial ring over \(\mathbb Z\) in the variables not selected by \(\lambda\), and is therefore an integral domain. Hence \(I_\lambda/K\) is prime in \(R/K\).

To prove minimality, let \(P/K\) be a prime ideal of \(R/K\) contained in \(I_\lambda/K\). Equivalently, \(P\) is a prime ideal of \(R\) with \(K\subseteq P\subseteq I_\lambda\). Since \(x_{2k+1}x_{2k+2}\in P\), primality gives
\[
x_{2k+1}\in P\quad\text{or}\quad x_{2k+2}\in P.
\]
Only \(\lambda_k\) belongs to \(I_\lambda\) among these two variables, so \(\lambda_k\in P\). This holds for every \(k\), hence \(I_\lambda\subseteq P\). Therefore \(P=I_\lambda\), proving that \(I_\lambda/K\) is minimal prime.

There are infinitely many distinct sequences \(\lambda\), and distinct sequences yield distinct ideals. Thus \(R/K\) has infinitely many minimal prime ideals.
\end{proof}
